title: Snoring, then retching
objective: Prioritize airway management and postoperative nausea and vomiting in the postanesthesia care unit, and give a clear handover from the surgical team

brief.situation: 10:40 in the postanesthesia care unit. Ms. Ferreira, 46, arrives after a two-hour laparoscopic gallbladder removal under general anesthesia. The anesthesia provider starts the handover at the bedside while she is still drowsy.
handover: She is snoring loudly, on a face mask; she had nausea and vomiting after her last anesthetic.
Orders: oxygen to keep SpO2 at or above 94%, the ordered IV antiemetic for nausea, the ordered IV opioid for pain over 6.

Unit policy: the receiving nurse takes a structured handover (procedure, airway, drugs given, fluids, problems, plan) with the anesthesia provider present, and calls anesthesia for any airway problem not fixed by basic maneuvers.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what comes first, what can wait, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: In what order do you handle her snoring, vomiting, pain and the handover, and why?

parts.label: Order
parts.criteria: Airway first (snoring with see-saw breathing is obstruction): jaw thrust, chin lift, oral or nasal airway, oxygen; then aspiration protection when she vomits (side, suction) and PONV treatment; pain once the airway is safe; the handover is taken with the anesthesia provider present.
parts.modelAnswer: Airway first: that snoring with see-saw breathing is obstruction, so jaw thrust, an airway adjunct and more oxygen. When she retches, turn her on her side and suction so she doesn't aspirate, and give the antiemetic. Pain comes once her airway is safe. I take the handover with anesthesia still at the bedside.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: A drowsy patient after volatile anesthetic and opioid with a PONV history has a high risk of obstruction and aspiration; an opioid into an obstructed airway worsens it.
parts.modelAnswer: She had a volatile anesthetic, an opioid and a history of PONV, and she's still drowsy, so obstruction and aspiration are the biggest risks. Giving the opioid before her airway is open would make it worse.

expertPath.text: Snoring with see-saw breathing: jaw thrust, nasal airway, more oxygen.
Structured handover with anesthesia at the bedside: PONV history, no antiemetic given.
Antiemetic. When she retches: on her side, suction.

aspiration.headline: Aspiration
aspiration.body: In the PACU the airway comes first: jaw thrust, an adjunct and oxygen for obstruction, then side and suction for vomiting. An opioid into an obstructed airway makes it worse.

recovered.headline: Airway first
recovered.body: You opened her airway at once, took a full handover, treated her PONV, protected her from aspiration and treated pain only once she was safe. That is the expert path.

recoveredGaps.headline: Recovered, with gaps
recoveredGaps.body: Check how fast you opened her airway, whether the handover happened with anesthesia present, and whether the opioid went in first.

time_up.headline: Unresolved
time_up.body: An obstructed airway in the PACU is fixed within a minute.

scoring.modelReasoning: Loud snoring with see-saw chest movement in a drowsy patient is upper airway obstruction: open it first with jaw thrust and chin lift, an oral or nasal airway if needed, and more oxygen. Her risk is high: a volatile anesthetic, an opioid, a two-hour case and a history of PONV. When she retches, turn her on her side and suction to prevent aspiration, and give the ordered antiemetic. Pain is treated once the airway is safe; an opioid into an obstructed airway worsens it. Take the structured handover with the anesthesia provider present and keep them until her airway is secure.
